title: Centipoise and Pascal-Seconds: Motor Oil Grades
h1: Centipoise and pascal-seconds — reading viscosity spec sheets
description: Motor oil is spec'd in SAE grades, but underneath is a real viscosity in centipoise or millipascal-seconds. Here is how the units and grades connect.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against SAE J300 and ASTM D2270

hero: 1 cP = 1 mPa·s exactly — the SI system quietly matched the CGS number so nobody had to relearn viscosity tables.
body: Dynamic viscosity is one of the few properties where CGS and SI units produce identical numbers. 1 centipoise = 1 millipascal-second, so a spec sheet can quote either without confusion. What confuses is the mapping to consumer grades — SAE 5W-30, ISO VG 46, AGMA 5 — none of which are viscosities themselves.

> 1 poise (P) = 0.1 Pa·s (exact)
> 1 centipoise (cP) = 1 mPa·s = 10⁻³ Pa·s
> Water at 20°C: 1.002 cP
> Motor oil 40°C: 30–100 cP
> Honey 25°C: 10,000 cP
> Kinematic: 1 stokes (St) = 10⁻⁴ m²/s; 1 cSt = 1 mm²/s

Dynamic viscosity (µ, cP or Pa·s) is the resistance to flow under an applied stress. Kinematic viscosity (ν, cSt or mm²/s) is µ divided by density. Oil datasheets list both because different measurement methods produce different natural outputs. ν = µ / ρ, always.

SAE J300 defines multigrade oils by two numbers. The 'W' number (5W, 10W, 15W) is a low-temperature pumpability spec measured in cP at −20 to −35°C. The second number (30, 40, 50) is a 100°C kinematic viscosity range in cSt: SAE 30 = 9.3–12.5 cSt; SAE 40 = 12.5–16.3 cSt; SAE 50 = 16.3–21.9 cSt. A 5W-30 must pass both a cold pump test and land in the 30-grade viscosity range hot.

ISO VG (Viscosity Grade) numbers the ISO 3448 mid-point kinematic viscosity at 40°C in cSt: ISO VG 32 = 28.8–35.2 cSt at 40°C. ISO VG 68, VG 100, VG 220 follow a 1.5× progression. This system is used for gear, hydraulic and turbine oils worldwide.

A hydraulic ram spec'd for ISO VG 46 oil operates at 60°C. ISO VG 46 at 40°C is 41.4–50.6 cSt. At 60°C (from a VI = 100 chart) it drops to roughly 22 cSt = 22 mm²/s. Density about 870 kg/m³, so dynamic viscosity µ = 22 × 10⁻⁶ × 870 = 0.0191 Pa·s = 19.1 cP. That figure feeds the Reynolds number for the ram's oil passages.
1 cP = 1 mPa·s. Kinematic viscosity (cSt) = dynamic / density. SAE and ISO grades map to specific cSt ranges — always check the datasheet's cSt at operating temperature.

faqs.a: Convenient coincidence. The centipoise was defined so that room-temperature water is (nearly) unity, making comparisons intuitive.
VI is a dimensionless number that describes how viscosity changes with temperature. Higher VI = flatter curve. Multigrade motor oils have VI 150–200; straight-grade oils, 90–100.

faqs.q: Does 5W-30 mean the oil is thinner cold?
faqs.a: It means it passes a cold pump test. Any oil is thicker cold; the 'W' rating specifies how thick it can be at low temperature.
